results.content:
## The PC

A desktop mini board, not a laptop: a mobile CPU (Ryzen 9 8945HX) on a mini-ITX-class board, and a mobile GPU chip
(GA106M, "RTX 3060 Laptop GPU") on a desktop PCIe card, the kind sold as a converted laptop GPU (subsystem ID
`10de:0000`, no OEM's). The model's experts live in system RAM; the GPU holds the dense layers, the KV cache and a
cache of experts (2666 of the Coder's, 1864 of UD-IQ4_XS's); the experts it does not hold are computed by the CPU
from RAM or copied to the GPU over PCIe (`--pcie-frac`). So the numbers that matter are the GPU's VRAM and memory
bandwidth, the PCIe link, the RAM's bandwidth and the CPU's cores. Read on 2026-10-03 with `lscpu`, `nvidia-smi -q`,
sysfs and `lspci`; "spec" marks a vendor figure, "measured" one measured on this PC.

**GPU**

| | |
|---|---|
| Card | NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3060 Laptop GPU, GA106M (`10de:2520`, rev a1), Ampere, compute capability 8.6; VBIOS 94.06.0F.00.AE |
| VRAM | 12288 MiB GDDR6; memory clock 7001 MHz (14 Gbps effective); 192-bit bus, 336 GB/s (spec for GA106 at 14 Gbps) |
| Cores, clocks | 30 SMs, 3840 CUDA cores (spec); graphics clock up to 2100 MHz, 1980 MHz seen under the BFCL load |
| Power | 80 W limit (default and current; the card allows 1-85 W); P0 under load; 60-64 °C at 100% load |
| PCIe link | **PCIe 4.0 x16** (16 GT/s, x16, the card's maximum; the slot can do 5.0): about 31.5 GB/s each way in theory |
| PCIe, measured | **26.8 GB/s host to device** (the engine's probe at every start, so `--pcie-frac 0.55`, the default) |
| BAR1 | 8192 MiB (less than the 12 GiB of VRAM) |
| Driver | 580.142, the official driver repacked by "FrankenDriver" for converted cards: same kernel module, plus `NVreg_RegistryDwords="RM1457588=1;"` (see `~/3060M-FrankenDriver-Linux.md`); GSP firmware on, persistence mode off, dynamic power management 3 |
| CUDA | 13.0 toolkit in the conda environment (nvcc 13.0.88, cuBLAS 13.1.1.3); the engine is built for sm_86 |

**CPU**

| | |
|---|---|
| CPU | AMD Ryzen 9 8945HX (Zen 4, mobile "HX"), 16 cores / 32 threads, 1 socket, 1 NUMA node |
| Layout | two chiplets: CCD1 = cores 0-7, CCD2 = cores 8-15; logical CPUs 16-31 are the SMT siblings of 0-15 |
| Caches | L1d 32 KiB + L1i 32 KiB per core, L2 1 MiB per core (16 MiB), L3 64 MiB (32 MiB per chiplet) |
| Vector | AVX2 and AVX-512 (F, BW, DQ, VL, CD, IFMA, VBMI, VBMI2, VNNI, **BF16**, BITALG, VPOPCNTDQ) |
| Clocks | 400-5461 MHz; measured under the BFCL load: 5083 MHz on CCD1, 4901 MHz on CCD2 |
| Power policy | `amd-pstate-epp`, governor `powersave`, energy preference `performance` |
| Strata's use | 15 expert-pool workers pinned to cores 1-15 and the host thread on core 0; SMT siblings left idle (see "Where the CPU time goes") |

**Memory**

| | |
|---|---|
| Modules | 2 x 48 GB DDR5 SO-DIMM, Crucial `CT48G56C46S5.M16B1` (manufacturer ID bank 6, 0x9B), dual rank, unbuffered, no ECC, 1.1 V |
| Channels | **dual channel**: one module on channel A, one on channel B (both slots used; the board takes up to 128 GB) |
| Speed | rated DDR5-5600 (CL46), **running at 5200 MT/s** (the 8945HX's supported maximum) |
| Bandwidth | 5200 MT/s x 8 bytes x 2 channels = **83.2 GB/s** in theory; **measured: about 55 GB/s read** (66%), see below |
| Seen by the OS | 98.8 GB (`free`), 92 GiB `MemTotal`; 2 GiB is the iGPU's carve-out (`mem_info_vram_total`) |
| Settings | swap 8 GiB file (3 MiB used); transparent huge pages `madvise`; no static huge pages |
| Page cache reads | the engine loads cached model files at 8.7-9.3 GiB/s (a single-threaded file read, not a bandwidth figure) |

Read with `sudo dmidecode -t memory` (saved as `~/dmi-memory.txt`).

**CPU memory bandwidth, measured** (2026-10-04, machine idle). A STREAM-style test in C with OpenMP
(`benchmarks/2026-10-04-3060m-membw.c`: `gcc -O3 -march=native -ffast-math -fopenmp`, AVX-512 code): three 2 GiB
arrays (far larger than the 64 MiB L3), best of 5 passes, threads pinned with `OMP_PLACES`/`OMP_PROC_BIND=close`.
Bytes are counted as STREAM counts them (what the code loads and stores):

| threads (cores) | read | write | copy | triad | memset (NT stores) | memcpy (NT stores) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 (core 1) | 46.2 | 24.9 | 31.4 | 35.8 | 62.3 | 36.2 |
| 2 (cores 1-2) | 51.4 | 24.8 | 34.1 | 37.9 | 65.4 | 46.4 |
| 4 (cores 1-4) | 50.9 | 24.1 | 32.4 | 36.6 | 59.1 | 48.5 |
| 8 (cores 1-8) | 52.0 | 24.2 | 31.5 | 35.5 | 57.0 | 49.1 |
| **15 (cores 1-15, Strata's workers)** | **54.6** | 24.1 | 30.9 | 34.6 | 55.2 | 48.2 |
| 16 (all cores) | 55.5 | 24.2 | 30.8 | 34.5 | 54.5 | 47.9 |
| 32 (with the SMT siblings) | 55.3 | 24.1 | 30.6 | 34.4 | 49.3 | 47.3 |
| 8, CCD1 only (cores 0-7) | 49.7 | 23.7 | 31.3 | 35.3 | 56.2 | 48.0 |
| 8, CCD2 only (cores 8-15) | 46.4 | 23.7 | 31.2 | 35.1 | 56.7 | 48.0 |
| 8, 4 on each chiplet | **57.0** | 24.7 | 31.6 | 35.4 | 56.1 | 50.0 |

GB/s; a repeat of the 15- and 16-thread rows came within 0.7 GB/s.

- **Read, what Strata's expert workers do** (they only read weights): about **55 GB/s** with 15-16 threads, 66% of
  the 83.2 GB/s theory; at most 57.0 with 4 threads on each chiplet. One thread already reaches 46 GB/s and 2-4
  reach 51: memory, not the number of cores, is the limit.
- **One chiplet** reads 46-50 GB/s, both together 55-57: each chiplet's Infinity Fabric link nearly fills the memory
  on its own, so spreading over both adds about 10%.
- **SMT siblings add nothing** (55.3 with 32 threads vs 55.5 with 16; memset drops from 54.5 to 49.3), which agrees
  with Strata leaving them idle.
- **Plain stores count half**: `write` and the stores in `copy`/`triad` first read each cache line
  (read-for-ownership), so 24 GB/s counted is about 48 GB/s of real traffic. Non-temporal stores (glibc's
  memset/memcpy at this size) skip that: 54-65 GB/s for writing.
- For comparison on this PC: the GPU's VRAM 336 GB/s (spec), the PCIe link 26.8 GB/s measured. The experts the GPU
  does not hold are read by the CPU at most at about 55 GB/s, or copied to the GPU at 26.8 GB/s.

**Storage and network**

| | |
|---|---|
| SSD | Acer SSD N3500 1 TB (MAXIO MAP1202, DRAM-less), **PCIe 3.0 x4** (8 GT/s x4: about 3.9 GB/s in theory); root on LVM, 688 GB free |
| Measured | the engine's expert load at start: 55.4 GiB of UD-IQ4_XS experts at 2.57-2.75 GiB/s (20-22 s), 23.4 GiB of Coder experts at 1.7-2.9 GiB/s - from the SSD, or partly from the page cache; when they are all cached: 8.7-9.3 GiB/s |
| Network share | `/mnt/evox2` (SMB): 112 MB/s measured with `rsync` (59.3 GB in 8 min 24 s; 93.7 GB in 13 min 16 s); loading a model straight from it ran at 0.11 GiB/s |

**System and software**

| | |
|---|---|
| Board | "Micro Computer (HK) Tech Limited" / "Meigao Innovation Technology", product `MotherBoard Series`, board `DRFXL`, BIOS 1.14 (2025-11-13); chassis type 3 = desktop |
| iGPU | AMD Raphael (Radeon 610M class), PCIe-attached at 16 GT/s x16; not used by Strata |
| OS | Ubuntu 24.04.4 LTS, Linux 6.8.0-136-generic, gcc 13.3.0 |
| Python | 3.14.7 in the conda environment `strata` (`~/miniconda3/envs/strata`); BFCL in `bfcl-py312` (Python 3.12) |
| Models | Qwen3.8-Flash-Next Coder IQ1_M (2 shards, 58.4 GB) and Unsloth UD-IQ4_XS (3 shards, 93.7 GB), in `~/Documents` |

## The PC

A desktop mini board, not a laptop: a mobile CPU (Ryzen 9 8945HX) on a mini-ITX-class board, and a mobile GPU chip
(GA106M, "RTX 3060 Laptop GPU") on a desktop PCIe card, the kind sold as a converted laptop GPU (subsystem ID
`10de:0000`, no OEM's). The model's experts live in system RAM; the GPU holds the dense layers, the KV cache and a
cache of experts (2666 of the Coder's, 1864 of UD-IQ4_XS's); the experts it does not hold are computed by the CPU
from RAM or copied to the GPU over PCIe (`--pcie-frac`). So the numbers that matter are the GPU's VRAM and memory
bandwidth, the PCIe link, the RAM's bandwidth and the CPU's cores. Read on 2026-10-03 with `lscpu`, `nvidia-smi -q`,
sysfs and `lspci`; "spec" marks a vendor figure, "measured" one measured on this PC.

**GPU**

| | |
|---|---|
| Card | NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3060 Laptop GPU, GA106M (`10de:2520`, rev a1), Ampere, compute capability 8.6; VBIOS 94.06.0F.00.AE |
| VRAM | 12288 MiB GDDR6; memory clock 7001 MHz (14 Gbps effective); 192-bit bus, 336 GB/s (spec for GA106 at 14 Gbps) |
| Cores, clocks | 30 SMs, 3840 CUDA cores (spec); graphics clock up to 2100 MHz, 1980 MHz seen under the BFCL load |
| Power | 80 W limit (default and current; the card allows 1-85 W); P0 under load; 60-64 °C at 100% load |
| PCIe link | **PCIe 4.0 x16** (16 GT/s, x16, the card's maximum; the slot can do 5.0): about 31.5 GB/s each way in theory |
| PCIe, measured | **26.8 GB/s host to device** (the engine's probe at every start, so `--pcie-frac 0.55`, the default) |
| BAR1 | 8192 MiB (less than the 12 GiB of VRAM) |
| Driver | 580.142, the official driver repacked by "FrankenDriver" for converted cards: same kernel module, plus `NVreg_RegistryDwords="RM1457588=1;"` (see `~/3060M-FrankenDriver-Linux.md`); GSP firmware on, persistence mode off, dynamic power management 3 |
| CUDA | 13.0 toolkit in the conda environment (nvcc 13.0.88, cuBLAS 13.1.1.3); the engine is built for sm_86 |

**CPU**

| | |
|---|---|
| CPU | AMD Ryzen 9 8945HX (Zen 4, mobile "HX"), 16 cores / 32 threads, 1 socket, 1 NUMA node |
| Layout | two chiplets: CCD1 = cores 0-7, CCD2 = cores 8-15; logical CPUs 16-31 are the SMT siblings of 0-15 |
| Caches | L1d 32 KiB + L1i 32 KiB per core, L2 1 MiB per core (16 MiB), L3 64 MiB (32 MiB per chiplet) |
| Vector | AVX2 and AVX-512 (F, BW, DQ, VL, CD, IFMA, VBMI, VBMI2, VNNI, **BF16**, BITALG, VPOPCNTDQ) |
| Clocks | 400-5461 MHz; measured under the BFCL load: 5083 MHz on CCD1, 4901 MHz on CCD2 |
| Power policy | `amd-pstate-epp`, governor `powersave`, energy preference `performance` |
| Strata's use | 15 expert-pool workers pinned to cores 1-15 and the host thread on core 0; SMT siblings left idle (see "Where the CPU time goes") |

**Memory**

| | |
|---|---|
| Modules | 2 x 48 GB DDR5 SO-DIMM, Crucial `CT48G56C46S5.M16B1` (manufacturer ID bank 6, 0x9B), dual rank, unbuffered, no ECC, 1.1 V |
| Channels | **dual channel**: one module on channel A, one on channel B (both slots used; the board takes up to 128 GB) |
| Speed | rated DDR5-5600 (CL46), **running at 5200 MT/s** (the 8945HX's supported maximum) |
| Bandwidth | 5200 MT/s x 8 bytes x 2 channels = **83.2 GB/s** in theory; **measured: about 55 GB/s read** (66%), see below |
| Seen by the OS | 98.8 GB (`free`), 92 GiB `MemTotal`; 2 GiB is the iGPU's carve-out (`mem_info_vram_total`) |
| Settings | swap 8 GiB file (3 MiB used); transparent huge pages `madvise`; no static huge pages |
| Page cache reads | the engine loads cached model files at 8.7-9.3 GiB/s (a single-threaded file read, not a bandwidth figure) |

Read with `sudo dmidecode -t memory` (saved as `~/dmi-memory.txt`).

**CPU memory bandwidth, measured** (2026-10-04, machine idle). A STREAM-style test in C with OpenMP
(`benchmarks/2026-10-04-3060m-membw.c`: `gcc -O3 -march=native -ffast-math -fopenmp`, AVX-512 code): three 2 GiB
arrays (far larger than the 64 MiB L3), best of 5 passes, threads pinned with `OMP_PLACES`/`OMP_PROC_BIND=close`.
Bytes are counted as STREAM counts them (what the code loads and stores):

| threads (cores) | read | write | copy | triad | memset (NT stores) | memcpy (NT stores) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 (core 1) | 46.2 | 24.9 | 31.4 | 35.8 | 62.3 | 36.2 |
| 2 (cores 1-2) | 51.4 | 24.8 | 34.1 | 37.9 | 65.4 | 46.4 |
| 4 (cores 1-4) | 50.9 | 24.1 | 32.4 | 36.6 | 59.1 | 48.5 |
| 8 (cores 1-8) | 52.0 | 24.2 | 31.5 | 35.5 | 57.0 | 49.1 |
| **15 (cores 1-15, Strata's workers)** | **54.6** | 24.1 | 30.9 | 34.6 | 55.2 | 48.2 |
| 16 (all cores) | 55.5 | 24.2 | 30.8 | 34.5 | 54.5 | 47.9 |
| 32 (with the SMT siblings) | 55.3 | 24.1 | 30.6 | 34.4 | 49.3 | 47.3 |
| 8, CCD1 only (cores 0-7) | 49.7 | 23.7 | 31.3 | 35.3 | 56.2 | 48.0 |
| 8, CCD2 only (cores 8-15) | 46.4 | 23.7 | 31.2 | 35.1 | 56.7 | 48.0 |
| 8, 4 on each chiplet | **57.0** | 24.7 | 31.6 | 35.4 | 56.1 | 50.0 |

GB/s; a repeat of the 15- and 16-thread rows came within 0.7 GB/s.

- **Read, what Strata's expert workers do** (they only read weights): about **55 GB/s** with 15-16 threads, 66% of
  the 83.2 GB/s theory; at most 57.0 with 4 threads on each chiplet. One thread already reaches 46 GB/s and 2-4
  reach 51: memory, not the number of cores, is the limit.
- **One chiplet** reads 46-50 GB/s, both together 55-57: each chiplet's Infinity Fabric link nearly fills the memory
  on its own, so spreading over both adds about 10%.
- **SMT siblings add nothing** (55.3 with 32 threads vs 55.5 with 16; memset drops from 54.5 to 49.3), which agrees
  with Strata leaving them idle.
- **Plain stores count half**: `write` and the stores in `copy`/`triad` first read each cache line
  (read-for-ownership), so 24 GB/s counted is about 48 GB/s of real traffic. Non-temporal stores (glibc's
  memset/memcpy at this size) skip that: 54-65 GB/s for writing.
- For comparison on this PC: the GPU's VRAM 336 GB/s (spec), the PCIe link 26.8 GB/s measured. The experts the GPU

results.content:
[TODO.md](TODO.md) item 2b: the expert products' MMQ kernels run at 6-12 TOPS at the expert shapes. The lead was
llama.cpp#21284's smaller tiles. Two premises were wrong. First, MMQ on gfx1151 does not use `sudot4`: the
vendored ggml defines `AMD_WMMA_AVAILABLE` for every gfx11 chip, and each kernel instance holds 276
`v_wmma_i32_16x16x16_iu8` instructions and no `v_dot4` (`llvm-objdump` on the gfx1151 code object of
`mmq-instance-{iq3_xxs,q2_0,iq4_nl}.cu`). `sudot4` is the path for cards without matrix cores. Second, the pinned
llama.cpp (3cf0325) is newer than #21284. It has one tile table per architecture (`mmq-config-rdna3-5.cuh`, 256
threads and I = 128 for J >= 48), and #21284's tile (128 threads, I = 64) is what the RDNA 3.0 table already uses.

**The harness** (`docs/benchmarks/2026-10-06-halo-mmq-tiles.cpp`, linking `strata_mmq.lib`; random weight bytes as in
TODO 2's harness) times each expert type two ways. "Uniform" is 512 experts of exactly J rows, groups of 16, the
tile for J: the kernel's own throughput at each tile. "Layer" is one 4,165-token layer as the engine runs it since
TODO 2a: Zipf-like rows, class-major, groups of 16 within a class, the tile for the group's median. The baseline
(`...-tiles-base.log`) showed two things. IQ3_XXS and IQ2_S (the Coder's gate/up) run *slower* at J = 128 than at
J = 112 (IQ3_XXS 9.8-9.9 against 12.5-13.1 TOPS). Most types run J = 32 no faster per operation than J = 16 (IQ4_XS
gate/up 6.5 against 7.6 TOPS). The compiler's resource report (`-Rpass-analysis=kernel-resource-usage`,
`...-mmq-registers.log`) explains both:

| VGPRs / scratch bytes per lane, default scheduler | J = 16 | J = 32 | J = 48-112 | J = 128 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| IQ3_XXS (Coder gate/up) | 195 / 0 | 256 / 16 | 191-237 / 0 | **256 / 208** |
| IQ2_S (Coder gate/up) | 256 / 28 | 186 / 0 | 213-256 / 0-56 | **256 / 132** |
| IQ4_NL, Q2_0 (Coder down) | 211 / 0 | **256 / 108** | 165-241 / 0 | 228-251 / 0 |
| IQ4_XS, IQ3_S, Q8_0 (UD-IQ4_XS) | 212-227 / 0 | **256 / 120-180** | 125-245 / 0 | 229-251 / 0 |

256 VGPRs is the most a wave32 kernel can have here; the rest spills to scratch memory. The spills do not come from
the tile's area: a thread holds J/2 accumulators whatever I is, and moving J = 32 to 256 threads / I = 128 still
spilled. They come from how LLVM's default scheduler orders the fully unrolled WMMA loop.

**What was tried** (the nine MMQ instances rebuilt with extra device flags and linked ahead of `strata_mmq.lib`;
"layer" ms per layer, 2-3 runs each, `...-tiles-variants.log`):

| ms per layer | IQ3_XXS g/u | IQ2_S g/u | IQ4_XS g/u | IQ3_S g/u | IQ4_NL down | Q2_0 down | IQ4_XS down | Q8_0 down |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| default scheduler | 28.1-28.2 | 30.9-33.7 | 25.1-25.7 | 28.4-28.5 | 15.1-15.5 | 15.3-15.6 | 10.8-11.2 | 15.6-15.8 |
| `-amdgpu-sched-strategy=iterative-minreg` (no spills, 104-239 VGPRs) | 33.0 | 39.6 | 33.3 | 33.9 | 19.5 | 17.9 | 14.6 | 20.2 |
| `-amdgpu-sched-strategy=max-memory-clause` | 26.3 | 30.8 | 24.7 | 28.6 | 15.0 | 14.8 | 11.0 | 15.9 |
| `-amdgpu-use-amdgpu-trackers=1` | 26.7 | 30.8 | 26.1 | 29.2 | 15.5 | 15.7 | 11.2 | 17.3 |
| `-unroll-threshold=50` (fixes most J = 32 spills) | 27.9 | 31.2 | 23.4 | 26.4 | 14.4 | 14.2 | 10.2 | 14.6 |
| **`-amdgpu-sched-strategy=max-ilp` (shipped)** | **25.8-25.9** | **30.1-30.7** | **22.6-23.1** | **26.4-26.8** | **14.1-14.4** | **14.1-14.3** | **10.2-10.5** | **14.8-15.0** |
| max-ilp + `-unroll-threshold=50` | 25.7-25.9 | 30.0-30.1 | 22.0-22.2 | 26.6 | 14.4 | 14.2-14.4 | 10.2 | 14.7-14.9 |
| max-ilp + the #21284 tiles (128 threads, I = 64, J >= 48) | 25.3-25.6 | 31.0-31.9 | 22.0-22.5 | 26.5-27.0 | 13.9-14.0 | 13.6-13.9 | 9.7-9.9 | 14.7-15.1 |

on the down products. It still spills a little (IQ3_XXS 72 bytes at J = 128 instead of 208, most J = 32 cases none),

**GPU kernel speed, measured** (2026-10-06, GPU otherwise idle). The prompt path's expert products run through
llama.cpp's MMQ kernels (int8 tensor cores, `strata_mmq` in `build/`). The harness is the Halo branch's
`benchmarks/2026-10-06-halo-mmq-tiles.cpp` (AIMAX395-ROCm) ported to CUDA as
`benchmarks/2026-10-06-3060m-mmq-tiles.cu`: `hip*` renamed to `cuda*`, and no `Product::opt_rows`, which this
branch does not have (here the tile follows the group's largest expert, there its median). Random weight bytes: the
time is real, the values are not. "Uniform": 512 experts of exactly J rows, groups of 16, the tile for J, the
kernel's own throughput. "Layer": one 4,165-token layer (41,650 rows, Zipf-like per expert, 3 seeds), class-major,
groups of 16 within a class, as the engine runs it. Two runs (`benchmarks/2026-10-06-3060m-mmq-tiles.log`):

| TOPS (2 x rows x cols x J) | J=16 | 32 | 48 | 64 | 80 | 96 | 112 | 128 | 256 | layer ms | layer TOPS |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| gate/up IQ3_XXS (Coder) | 7.9 | 13.9-16.3 | 18.9-21.6 | 25.8 | 27.5-27.8 | 29.9-30.1 | 32.1 | 33.5-33.7 | 33.5-33.6 | 12.1 | 22.5 |
| gate/up IQ2_S (Coder) | 10.0-10.2 | 14.0-14.1 | 18.7 | 21.4 | 24.6-24.7 | 25.8-25.9 | 27.2 | 28.2 | 28.5 | 13.9 | 19.6-19.7 |
| gate/up IQ4_XS (UD-IQ4_XS) | 12.1 | 18.8-18.9 | 24.9-25.0 | 28.1-28.3 | 30.8 | 33.3-33.4 | 34.5-34.6 | 35.8 | 36.7-36.8 | 10.9 | 25.1 |
| gate/up IQ3_S (UD-IQ4_XS) | 9.5-9.6 | 14.4 | 20.6 | 24.2 | 26.7 | 29.3-29.4 | 31.0 | 32.7 | 32.6 | 12.6 | 21.6-21.7 |
| down IQ4_NL (Coder) | 10.0 | 15.2-15.3 | 16.3-16.9 | 19.5-19.9 | 20.9-21.0 | 24.2 | 25.0-25.1 | 25.8-25.9 | 26.4-26.5 | 7.5 | 18.2 |
| down Q2_0 (Coder) | 13.6-13.7 | 19.1-19.2 | 23.5-23.6 | 19.9-20.2 | 22.5 | 24.8 | 25.9-26.0 | 27.2 | 27.4-27.6 | 6.7 | 20.2-20.3 |
| down IQ4_XS (UD-IQ4_XS) | 15.0-15.1 | 23.1-23.3 | 24.1-25.2 | 27.1-27.4 | 29.4-29.6 | 32.4-32.5 | 32.8-32.9 | 35.6 | 37.1-37.2 | 5.3 | 25.7-25.9 |
| down Q8_0 (UD-IQ4_XS) | 6.0 | 11.3 | 14.2 | 17.0 | 18.3 | 21.2-21.3 | 22.2-22.3 | 23.1 | 25.2 | 8.4-8.5 | 16.1-16.2 |

- **The kernels' peak on this card: 37 TOPS** (down IQ4_XS at 256 rows per expert; gate/up IQ4_XS 36.8), 33-36 TOPS
  for most types at J = 128, 25-28 for IQ2_S, IQ4_NL, Q2_0 and Q8_0. The two runs agree within 1% except IQ3_XXS
  at J = 32-48 (13.9 vs 16.3, 18.9 vs 21.6).
- **Small tiles are slow**: J = 16 reaches 6-15 TOPS, a quarter to a half of J = 128. Q2_0 down is slower at J = 64
  than at 48 (about 20 vs 23.5, both runs).
- **One layer runs at 16-26 TOPS**, 60-70% of the uniform J = 128 speed. The experts above 128 rows hold 52% of
  the rows (21,591) and take 37-43% of the layer's time; those of 17-32 rows hold 13% and take 19-22%.
- Clocks during the run (`nvidia-smi` every 200 ms): SM 1582-1762 MHz, mean 1656, not the 2100 MHz maximum;
  35 W mean, 38.6 W at most, under the 80 W limit; memory at 7001 MHz. Every sample reports the throttle reason
  0x4 ("SW power cap") although the draw is far below the limit; not explained yet.
- Against the int8 tensor cores' peak: GA10x does 2,048 dense int8 operations per clock per SM (from NVIDIA's RTX
  3090 figure: 284 TOPS, 82 SMs, 1695 MHz), so 30 SMs give 102 TOPS at the 1656 MHz measured (129 at 2100 MHz).
  37 TOPS is 36% of that.
- Against the Halo (Radeon 8060S, gfx1151, same harness, same layer, tile for the median): 25.8-30.7 ms per layer
  for the four gate/up types and 10.2-15.0 ms for the four down types with its shipped `max-ilp` build
  (`AIMAX+395-ROCm.md` on that branch); here 10.9-13.9 and 5.3-8.5 ms, about 2-2.4 times faster.

**Storage and network**

llama.cpp's MMQ kernels (int8 tensor cores, `strata_mmq` in `build/`). The harness is the Halo branch's
`benchmarks/2026-10-06-halo-mmq-tiles.cpp` (AIMAX395-ROCm) ported to CUDA as

branch does not have (here the tile follows the group's largest expert, there its median). Random weight bytes: the
time is real, the values are not. "Uniform": 512 experts of exactly J rows, groups of 16, the tile for J, the
kernel's own throughput. "Layer": one 4,165-token layer (41,650 rows, Zipf-like per expert, 3 seeds), class-major,
groups of 16 within a class, as the engine runs it. Two runs (`benchmarks/2026-10-06-3060m-mmq-tiles.log`):

| gate/up IQ3_S (UD-IQ4_XS) | 9.5-9.6 | 14.4 | 20.6 | 24.2 | 26.7 | 29.3-29.4 | 31.0 | 32.7 | 32.6 | 12.6 | 21.6-21.7 |
| down IQ4_NL (Coder) | 10.0 | 15.2-15.3 | 16.3-16.9 | 19.5-19.9 | 20.9-21.0 | 24.2 | 25.0-25.1 | 25.8-25.9 | 26.4-26.5 | 7.5 | 18.2 |
| down Q2_0 (Coder) | 13.6-13.7 | 19.1-19.2 | 23.5-23.6 | 19.9-20.2 | 22.5 | 24.8 | 25.9-26.0 | 27.2 | 27.4-27.6 | 6.7 | 20.2-20.3 |
| down IQ4_XS (UD-IQ4_XS) | 15.0-15.1 | 23.1-23.3 | 24.1-25.2 | 27.1-27.4 | 29.4-29.6 | 32.4-32.5 | 32.8-32.9 | 35.6 | 37.1-37.2 | 5.3 | 25.7-25.9 |
| down Q8_0 (UD-IQ4_XS) | 6.0 | 11.3 | 14.2 | 17.0 | 18.3 | 21.2-21.3 | 22.2-22.3 | 23.1 | 25.2 | 8.4-8.5 | 16.1-16.2 |

- **The kernels' peak on this card: 37 TOPS** (down IQ4_XS at 256 rows per expert; gate/up IQ4_XS 36.8), 33-36 TOPS
  for most types at J = 128, 25-28 for IQ2_S, IQ4_NL, Q2_0 and Q8_0. The two runs agree within 1% except IQ3_XXS
  at J = 32-48 (13.9 vs 16.3, 18.9 vs 21.6).
- **Small tiles are slow**: J = 16 reaches 6-15 TOPS, a quarter to a half of J = 128. Q2_0 down is slower at J = 64
  than at 48 (about 20 vs 23.5, both runs).
- **One layer runs at 16-26 TOPS**, 60-70% of the uniform J = 128 speed. The experts above 128 rows hold 52% of
  the rows (21,591) and take 37-43% of the layer's time; those of 17-32 rows hold 13% and take 19-22%.

  35 W mean, 38.6 W at most, under the 80 W limit; memory at 7001 MHz. Every sample reports the throttle reason
  0x4 ("SW power cap") although the draw is far below the limit; not explained yet.

  3090 figure: 284 TOPS, 82 SMs, 1695 MHz), so 30 SMs give 102 TOPS at the 1656 MHz measured (129 at 2100 MHz).

steps.message:
I measured the MMQ kernel peak on this machine with the Halo benchmark: **about 37 TOPS**. The results are in a new "GPU kernel speed, measured" part of `## The PC` in `docs/3060M.md`, just before "Storage and network". I ran it twice, and the two runs agree within 1% except IQ3_XXS at J=32–48.

**Changes needed to compile.** The original `.cpp` is HIP code and couldn't build here, so I made a CUDA copy on this branch: `docs/benchmarks/2026-10-06-3060m-mmq-tiles.cu`. Two changes:
- All `hip*` calls renamed to `cuda*`, and the device line prints `sm_86` instead of `gcnArchName`.
- I removed `p.opt_rows`. That field only exists on AIMAX395-ROCm, where the tile is chosen for the group's median expert size. This branch has no such field and always chooses the tile for the largest expert. You said to change only the copied file, so I didn't port the engine change.

  The "uniform" test is unaffected, because every expert there is the same size. The "layer" test measures this branch's own tile choice, so it isn't an exact match for the Halo setup.

The build command is in the file header. It links against `build/libstrata_mmq.a` and `build/ggml/src/libggml-base.a`, and the run takes 9 s.

**Results:**
- **Peak:** 37.2 TOPS on down IQ4_XS at 256 rows per expert. Gate/up IQ4_XS reaches 36.8. Most types reach 33–36 TOPS at J=128; IQ2_S, IQ4_NL, Q2_0 and Q8_0 reach 25–28.
- **Small tiles are slow:** J=16 gives only 6–15 TOPS. Q2_0 down is slower at J=64 than at J=48 in both runs.
- **One full layer:** 16–26 TOPS (5.3–13.9 ms), which is 66–75% of the uniform J=128 speed.
- **Against the hardware maximum:** I estimated the card's int8 tensor-core peak at 102 TOPS at the 1656 MHz measured. That figure is scaled from NVIDIA's published RTX 3090 number, not measured here. The kernels reach 36% of it.
- **Against the Halo:** its shipped `max-ilp` build is 1.7–2.2× slower per expert type on the same harness, though the tile choice differs as noted above.

**Unexplained:** the SM clock stayed at 1582–1762 MHz, not the 2100 MHz maximum. Power draw was only about 35 W against the 80 W limit, yet `nvidia-smi` reported the "SW power cap" throttle reason in every sample. The doc records this as not yet explained.

The raw output of both runs is in `docs/benchmarks/2026-10-06-3060m-mmq-tiles.log`. `.gitignore` excludes `*.log`, so committing it needs `git add -f`, which is how the logs on the Halo branch were added. Nothing is committed yet.

raw_arguments.description: Port GEMM variants benchmark to cuBLAS, build and run

steps.reasoning_content: I found the "compute 16F" row (661 TFLOP/s) is bogus because cuBLAS reads alpha/beta as `__half` under `CUBLAS_COMPUTE_16F`, so the float 1.0f gets read as half 0 and the GEMM is skipped (hipBLAS has the same issue, so the original has this bug too). I'll fix the copy by passing `__half` scalars for that case, then rerun it 3 times to check whether case order affects results since early rows may be slow from clock ramp-up.

arguments.description: Fix half scalars, rebuild, run three times with clock log

results.content:
The work list, in the order of the time at stake: the expert GEMMs (2.9 s with their dequant: a grouped GEMM or
a fixed MMQ), the prompt attention on gfx11 WMMA (1.9 s), the dense GEMMs' library efficiency (4 TFLOP/s against
the card's matrix-core peak), the GDN recurrence (0.8 s; llama.cpp's chunked form gained it 8% of a whole prompt
on this card).

## A better GEMM: what was searched, what was measured, what it gave (2026-10-05, evening)

**First, the clock.** A search turns up a Windows Strix Halo problem that would explain a 4 TFLOP/s GEMM
outright: the GPU drops to ~600 MHz for compute whenever the console display is off (lid closed, display
timeout), FP16 GEMM 31 -> 8 TFLOPS ([ROCm/legacy-rocm-build #6675](https://github.com/ROCm/legacy-rocm-build/issues/6675);
workarounds: `SetThreadExecutionState(ES_DISPLAY_REQUIRED)` in the process, or an injected 1-pixel mouse move).
This PC is driven over RDP with a 4K panel on the 8060S and a 300 s display timeout. Measured with
`docs/benchmarks/2026-10-05-halo-hip-clock.hip` (the 20-bit `SHADER_CYCLES` register over 100 us windows of the
100 MHz wall clock; gfx11 has no `s_memtime`, so `clock64()` reads 0): **2,780-2,900 MHz** under a spin load,
2,240-2,950 MHz while the hipBLASLt GEMM probe ran. Not throttled here, and the benchmark rows measured minutes
apart agree with each other. The risk stays for unattended runs longer than the display timeout; the engine does
not hold a display request.

**Second, the library, by variant** (`docs/benchmarks/2026-10-05-halo-gemm-variants.cpp`: `hipblasGemmEx` on
constant nonzero data, 10 timed calls, `ROCBLAS_USE_HIPBLASLT=1`; rocBLAS alone is 20-45% lower on every row):

| shape, layout, types | TFLOP/s |
|---|---|
| the engine's dense shape N=3072 T=8192 K=2048, T/N, **BF16 or FP16 in -> FP32 out** | **4.3** |
| the same, FP16 -> FP16 out, or BF16 -> BF16 out | **23.6-24.0** |
| N/N layout, FP16 -> FP32 / FP16 -> FP16 | 5.3 / 20.3 |
| 4096^3, FP16 -> FP32 / FP16 -> FP16 / BF16 -> BF16 | 4.3 / 25.4 / 26.1 |
| the expert shape N=1280 T=160 K=2560, FP16 -> FP32 / FP16 -> FP16 | 3.5 / 18.7 |
| the expert down shape N=2560 T=160 K=640, FP16 -> FP32 | 3.7 |
| decode-like N=3072 T=8 K=2048, FP16 -> FP32 | 1.0 |

So the slow path is one thing: **a 32-bit output**. With a 16-bit output the same library runs 5-6x faster on this
card, 24-26 TFLOP/s, which is the 32-37 TFLOP/s others measure on gfx1151 with hipBLASLt on big shapes
([llm-tracker](https://llm-tracker.info/AMD-Strix-Halo-(Ryzen-AI-Max+-395)-GPU-Performance): 36.9 peak, "59.4
theoretical"), less the FP32 accumulate and this shape. Every `cublasGemmEx` the engine issues asks for FP32 out
(`gemm.cu:388/407`), because the consumers accumulate into FP32 (`beta`, the hi/lo split GEMMs). A 16-bit output
with a cast would cap those at 11 bits: a numerical change for the maintainers, not a setting. `hipBLASLt`'s
`compute 16F` variant is faster still on rocBLAS (17 TFLOP/s) but accumulates in FP16: 1.2e-2 relative error
against 3.3e-4, unusable here. Checked with `docs/benchmarks/2026-10-05-halo-gemm-f16out.cpp` on random data.

**Third, the engine's own answer to this: its hipBLASLt solution table.** `tools/hip/tune_hipblaslt` asks
hipBLASLt for every heuristic solution of each of the engine's 32 dense GEMM shapes (T = 4096 and 8192), times
them against `hipblasGemmEx`, checks them against it (finite, max abs, relative L2 tolerances) and writes the
best ids. On gfx1151 with hipBLASLt 1.4.1 (60 s): **every shape found a 5.2-5.4x faster solution with FP32
output** (f16 T=8192 N=12288 K=2560: 201.0 -> 38.4 ms, 2.6 -> 13.4 TFLOP/s; T=4096: 101.5 -> 18.9 ms; the
96x96x32 macro-tile `SAV` kernels), shipped as `tools/hip/gfx1151-hipblaslt-100401.txt` (setup uses it when the
installed hipBLASLt reports 1.4.1; the configs here carry `STRATA_HIPBLASLT_TUNING`). The engine with the table:

| Coder IQ1_M, arena mode (the first two columns at 64/64, the table column at 32/96: the split the BIOS was left on after the UD-IQ4_XS runs; the cache held all 12,288 experts and hit 100% in every run either way) | plain | `ROCBLAS_USE_HIPBLASLT=1` | **the table** (+ the switch for the shapes it lacks) |
|---|---|---|---|
| pp4096 (`pp4k.py`, 2 requests) | 199-207 t/s | 264-279 t/s | **404-452 t/s** |
| 4,165-token prompt, GPU timeline | 19,955 ms | 14,725 ms | **9,188 ms** |
| hc read / GDN projections / QSA proj / router | 3,438 / 4,969 / 2,077 / 909 ms | 1,768 / 3,263 / 1,443 / 591 | **673 / 938 / 468 / 274** |
| QSA attn / expert GEMMs gate-up + down / dequant | 1,986 / 1,772 + 785 / 489 | 1,944 / 1,705 + 763 / 473 | 2,034 / 1,803 + 798 / 482 (untouched: not in the table) |
| the benchmark, prefill @ 4.75K / pp4096 / 16K prefix / 20K | 209 / 209 / 213 / 211 | 274 / 268 / 277 / 274 | **451 / 441 / 440 / 434 t/s** |
| the benchmark, decode (cold / fresh / after 4.75K / tg128 @ 16K) | 35.0 / 33.0 / 31.3 / 27.5 | 38.6 / 35.1 / 34.7 / 28.8 | 39.9 / 36.1 / 30.9 / 29.2 |

arguments.new_string:
(`AIMAX+395-ROCm.md` on that branch); here 10.9-13.9 and 5.3-8.5 ms, 1.7-2.2 times faster per type (the tile choice differs, see above).

**cuBLAS GEMM speed, measured** (2026-10-06, GPU otherwise idle). The Halo branch's
`benchmarks/2026-10-05-halo-gemm-variants.cpp` (`GemmEx` across input/output types, layouts and shapes, constant
nonzero data, 10 timed calls, 200 for the small shapes) ported to cuBLAS as
`benchmarks/2026-10-05-3060m-gemm-variants.cu`: `hip*` renamed, and the `compute 16F` row given `__half`
alpha/beta (cuBLAS reads them in the compute type; with the original's float 1.0 it read 0, skipped the product and
reported 661 TFLOP/s). Three runs back to back (`benchmarks/2026-10-06-3060m-gemm-variants.log`); the table gives
runs 2-3, as run 1's first three rows were still on a rising clock (20.3-23.7 TFLOP/s). SM clock 1935-2017 MHz.

| shape, layout, types | 3060M TFLOP/s | Halo (gfx1151, hipBLAS + hipBLASLt) |
|---|---|---|
| the engine's dense shape N=3072 T=8192 K=2048, T/N, **BF16 or FP16 in -> FP32 out** | **28.0-28.1** | 4.3 |
| the same, FP16 -> FP16 out / BF16 -> BF16 out | 29.0-29.1 / 28.8-29.0 | 23.6-24.0 |
| the same, FP16 -> FP16, compute 16F (FP16 accumulate) | 37.4-38.6 | - |
| N/N layout, FP16 -> FP32 / FP16 -> FP16 | 27.7-27.8 / 28.3 | 5.3 / 20.3 |
| 4096^3, T/N FP16 -> FP32 / N/N FP16 -> FP16 / T/N BF16 -> BF16 | 26.6-26.7 / 27.4-27.5 / 28.2 | 4.3 / 25.4 / 26.1 |
| the expert shape N=1280 T=160 K=2560, FP16 -> FP32 / FP16 -> FP16 | 22.2 / 21.8-22.2 | 3.5 / 18.7 |
| the expert down shape N=2560 T=160 K=640, FP16 -> FP32 | 10.6 | 3.7 |
| decode-like N=3072 T=8 K=2048, FP16 -> FP32 | 2.0 | 1.0 |

- **No FP32-output penalty here**: FP32 out runs at 96-97% of 16-bit out on the engine's shape (28.0 vs 29.0),
  where the Halo's hipBLAS loses 5-6x. Every `cublasGemmEx` the engine issues asks for FP32 out, so this card needs
  no tuning table for it.
- **The library is near the card's limit**: GeForce Ampere does FP16/BF16 with FP32 accumulate at 512 operations
  per clock per SM (from NVIDIA's RTX 3090 figure: 71 TFLOPS, 82 SMs, 1695 MHz), 30.4 TFLOP/s for 30 SMs at
  1980 MHz. 28-29 TFLOP/s is 92-95% of that. FP16 accumulate is twice the rate (60.8); 37-39 TFLOP/s measured,
  and the Halo branch found FP16 accumulate too inexact for the engine (1.2e-2 relative error against 3.3e-4).
- **The small shapes take 47-51 us each** whatever their size: the expert gate/up (1.05 GFLOP) 22 TFLOP/s, the
  down (0.52 GFLOP) 10.6, decode-like (0.10 GFLOP) 2.0. The decode-like call reads 12.6 MB of weights in 50 us,
  252 GB/s, 75% of the VRAM's 336 GB/s.
- Against the int8 MMQ above (37 TOPS at best, 16-26 TOPS per layer): the FP16 GEMM at an expert's shape gives
  22 TFLOP/s, but the engine's experts stay quantized for MMQ, which reads each 0.5-1.7 MB expert once instead of a
  dequantized FP16 copy.

**Storage and network**

steps.message:
I ran `2026-10-05-halo-gemm-variants.cpp` on this card. It's now a new part of `## The PC` in `docs/3060M.md`, "cuBLAS GEMM speed, measured", with the Halo's numbers next to mine.

**The copy:** `docs/benchmarks/2026-10-05-3060m-gemm-variants.cu`. Renaming `hip*` to `cu*` compiled cleanly, but one row came out wrong. For the `compute 16F` case, cuBLAS reads alpha/beta as `__half`. The original passes a float 1.0, which cuBLAS read as 0, so it skipped the multiply and reported 661 TFLOP/s. I pass `__half` values for that case only; the build command and this note are in the file header.

I ran it 3 times back to back. In run 1 the first three rows were 20–23 TFLOP/s because the clock was still ramping up. Runs 2 and 3 agree within 1–3%, and the table uses those. The SM clock was 1935–2017 MHz during the GEMMs.

**Results:**

| Engine's shape N=3072 T=8192 K=2048 | 3060M | Halo |
|---|---|---|
| BF16/FP16 in → FP32 out | **28.0** TFLOP/s | 4.3 |
| FP16 → FP16 out | 29.0 | 23.6–24.0 |
| FP16 accumulate (compute 16F) | 37.4–38.6 | – |

- **No penalty for FP32 output here.** FP32 out runs at 96–97% of the speed of 16-bit out. On the Halo, FP32 out is 5–6× slower, which is why it needed its hipBLASLt tuning table. This card doesn't.
- **cuBLAS is close to the card's limit.** 28–29 TFLOP/s is 92–95% of the FP16 tensor-core peak with FP32 accumulate (30.4 TFLOP/s at 1980 MHz). I scaled that peak from NVIDIA's published RTX 3090 figure; it isn't measured here.
- **Small shapes all take 47–51 µs, whatever their size:**
  - expert gate/up: 22 TFLOP/s
  - expert down: 10.6 TFLOP/s
  - decode-like: 2.0 TFLOP/s, i.e. 252 GB/s of weight reads, 75% of the VRAM's 336 GB/s

The raw output is in `docs/benchmarks/2026-10-06-3060m-gemm-variants.log`. Like the MMQ log, it is excluded by `.gitignore` and needs `git add -f` to commit. Nothing is committed yet.

steps.message:
I staged both logs with `git add -f`:
- `docs/benchmarks/2026-10-06-3060m-mmq-tiles.log`
- `docs/benchmarks/2026-10-06-3060m-gemm-variants.log`

My other changes were not lost. The repo has an automatic per-turn commit that already committed the `docs/3060M.md` edits and both `.cu` files. The MMQ test went into `8b101ed` and the GEMM test into `0587db4`. That commit used a plain `git add`, which skips `.log` files, so the logs were left out until now. They are only staged, not committed yet. If the automatic commit works the same way next turn, it should include them.

One thing to check: `8b101ed` also committed `docs/._3060M.md`, a 4 KB macOS metadata file (AppleDouble), probably created when the doc was opened over a network share. It isn't part of the docs. If you agree, I can run `git rm` on it and add `._*` to `.gitignore`.
